I passed several funeral processions, each with only a few mourners. People watching saw them as signs of terrible things to come. Some stared with a wild eagerness; others hurried away in fear; some cried aloud.

After arranging immediate help for the sick, Adrian’s main effort had been to hide the signs and spread of the plague from London’s people. He knew that fear and gloomy expectations helped disease take hold, and that despair and constant worry made the body especially vulnerable to infection. So no distressing sights were visible. Most shops stayed open, and there were still some people in the streets. Yet although London did not look like a plague-stricken city, it seemed greatly changed to me, since I had not seen it since the outbreak began. There were no carriages, and tall grass grew in the streets. The houses looked abandoned, with most shutters closed. The people I passed wore pale, frightened expressions, so unlike Londoners’ usual busy manner. My lone carriage drew attention as it rattled toward the Protector’s Palace. The fashionable streets around it looked even emptier and more depressing. I found Adrian’s waiting room crowded, for this was the hour when he received visitors. Unwilling to interrupt his work, I waited and watched people come and go. They were from the middle and lower classes, and had lost their livelihoods when trade and all the various forms of money-making so characteristic of our country had stopped. Those arriving looked anxious and sometimes terrified. Their faces were strikingly different from the calm, even satisfied expressions of those who had already seen him. In their livelier movements and happier faces I could see my friend’s influence. At two o’clock, no more people were admitted. Those who had missed their chance left in sadness or resentment, and I entered the room where Adrian received them.

I was struck by how much healthier he looked. He no longer drooped like a pampered spring flower that has grown beyond its strength and bends beneath the weight of its own blossoms. His eyes were bright, his face calm. His whole bearing showed a focused energy quite unlike his old weakness. He sat at a table with several secretaries, who were sorting requests or recording the notes taken during that day’s meetings. Two or three people were still waiting for help. I admired his fairness and patience. Anyone who could support themselves outside London was advised to leave immediately, and he provided the means for them to do so.

“Besides, this is a knot that scarcely anyone but a sailor knows how to tie, and it is characteristic of the Maltese. I found the ribbon at the base of the lightning-rod. It cannot have been the property of either dead woman. Now, even supposing my inference from the ribbon is mistaken, and the Frenchman is not a sailor on a Maltese ship, the statement in my advertisement can do no harm. If I am wrong, he will simply think some circumstance has deceived me, and will hardly trouble himself to investigate it. If I am correct, however, we gain a considerable advantage. Knowing of the murders, though innocent of them, the Frenchman will naturally hesitate to answer the notice and claim the Ourang-Outang. His reasoning will run like this: ‘I am innocent and poor; my Ourang-Outang is enormously valuable—a fortune to a man in my position. Why forfeit it because of groundless fears? It lies within my reach. It was discovered in the Bois de Boulogne, very far from the place of the slaughter. Who would suspect a brute animal of committing such an act? The police are baffled; they have not obtained the smallest clue. Even if they tracked the creature down, they could not prove that I knew of the murders, or establish my guilt merely because I knew. Above everything, my identity is known. The person advertising identifies me as the animal’s owner. I cannot tell how much more he knows. If I fail to reclaim such valuable property, when my ownership is known, I shall at least expose the creature to suspicion. My interest is to draw attention to neither myself nor it. I shall answer the notice, recover the Ourang-Outang, and keep it hidden until the affair has blown over.’”

Just then we heard a footstep on the staircase.

“Have your pistols ready,” Dupin said, “but do not display or use them unless I give the signal.”

The house’s outer door had been left ajar. Our visitor had come in without ringing and climbed several stairs, but now appeared to falter. After a moment we heard him going down. Dupin moved swiftly toward the door, just as the steps began ascending again. This time the man did not retreat, but came up resolutely and knocked at our room.

“Come in,” Dupin called in a warm, cheerful voice.

A man entered, plainly a sailor: tall, heavily built, and muscular, with a certain reckless boldness in his face that was not altogether unattractive.

“Allow me to point out, Sir Walter,” Mr. Shepherd said one morning at Kellynch Hall, setting down the newspaper, “that the present situation is very much in our favor. This peace will bring all our wealthy naval officers ashore, and every one of them will want a home. There couldn’t be a better moment, Sir Walter, to have your choice of tenants, thoroughly reliable tenants. Many impressive fortunes were made during the war. If a rich admiral should happen to come our way, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very fortunate man, Shepherd,” Sir Walter replied. “That is all I have to say. Kellynch Hall would be quite a prize for him, indeed the greatest of his prizes, however many he has captured before. Wouldn’t it, Shepherd?”

Mr. Shepherd laughed at the joke, as he knew he was expected to, and continued:

“I venture to say, Sir Walter, that naval gentlemen are agreeable people to do business with. I have some experience of their business practices, and I freely admit that they are generous in their dealings and as likely to make excellent tenants as any group one could encounter. So what I would respectfully suggest, Sir Walter, is this: if any rumors of your plans were to circulate—and we must recognize that possibility, since everyone knows how difficult it is to shield one part of the world’s affairs from the curiosity of the other; distinction has its price; I, John Shepherd, could keep any family business private because no one would consider me worth watching, but Sir Walter Elliot attracts an attention that may be very hard to escape—therefore, I venture to say that, despite all our precautions, I would not be very surprised if some hint of the truth got out. In that event, as I was about to observe, inquiries would certainly follow, and I would consider any from wealthy naval commanders particularly deserving of attention. And allow me to add that I can be here within two hours at any time, to spare you the trouble of answering them.”

Sir Walter merely nodded. Soon afterward, however, he stood up and paced the room, remarking sarcastically:

“I imagine very few naval gentlemen would fail to be surprised at finding themselves in a house of this kind.”

“They would certainly look around and count themselves fortunate,” Mrs. Clay said. She was present because her father had driven her over; nothing benefited Mrs. Clay’s health so much as a drive to Kellynch. “But I entirely agree with my father that a sailor could be a most desirable tenant.”
